purpose: Evidence-reviewed clinical additions and replacements for the generated UKMLA card dataset.

conditions.name: Urinary tract infection

fields.investigations: Clinical diagnosis. Do not use urine dipsticks to diagnose UTI in adults aged 65 years or over or in people with an indwelling urinary catheter. Send urine culture when indicated, including men, pregnancy, recurrent/atypical UTI, pyelonephritis, treatment failure and suspected catheter-associated UTI; obtain before antibiotics where feasible.
fields.treatment: Uncomplicated lower UTI in a non-pregnant younger woman: follow current local/NICE antimicrobial guidance, commonly nitrofurantoin if renal function is suitable. In older or catheterised adults, treat only when compatible clinical features support infection; do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.
fields.escalation: Same-day/urgent assessment for pyelonephritis or sepsis, pregnancy with systemic illness, AKI, obstruction/retention, catheter-associated systemic illness, inability to maintain oral intake or marked clinical deterioration.
fields.mimics: STI/urethritis, vaginitis, overactive bladder, interstitial cystitis, stones, bladder cancer and prostatitis; in older adults also consider pneumonia/other infection, dehydration, constipation, urinary retention, pain, medication effects and metabolic causes of delirium.
fields.redFlags: Fever or hypothermia, flank pain, rigors, vomiting, hypotension, AKI/oliguria, obstruction/retention, visible haematuria or systemic deterioration. New delirium in a frail older adult warrants urgent assessment, but delirium or bacteriuria alone does not diagnose UTI.

sourceReview: NICE NG109: Lower UTI antimicrobial prescribing
NICE NG113: Catheter-associated UTI antimicrobial prescribing
SAPG: UTI decision aids for people aged 65 years and over

conditions.name: Polycystic ovary syndrome
conditions.newName: Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS; formerly PCOS)

fields.investigations: Adults: after excluding alternatives, diagnose with 2 of 3 — ovulatory dysfunction/irregular cycles, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, or polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound or elevated AMH. If irregular cycles plus hyperandrogenism are already present, ultrasound/AMH is not required. In adolescents require both irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism; do not use ultrasound or AMH diagnostically. Assess BP/lipids and glycaemia; a 75-g OGTT is the most accurate glycaemic test.
fields.treatment: Lifestyle management and long-term metabolic risk reduction; COCP can treat irregular cycles/hirsutism if suitable. Consider metformin primarily for metabolic indications, especially in adults with BMI ≥25 kg/m²; letrozole is first-line pharmacological ovulation induction when infertility due to anovulation is the issue, usually specialist-led.
fields.escalation: Refer endocrine/gynae for rapid or severe virilisation, markedly elevated androgens, diagnostic uncertainty, infertility requiring treatment, prolonged amenorrhoea/endometrial-risk concerns or major metabolic complications.
fields.mimics: Androgen-secreting ovarian/adrenal tumour, ovarian hyperthecosis, non-classic CAH, Cushing syndrome, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease, severe insulin-resistance syndromes, hypothalamic amenorrhoea and exogenous androgens.
fields.redFlags: Rapid-onset virilisation, deepening voice/clitoromegaly, new severe androgen excess after menopause, pelvic/adrenal mass, markedly elevated testosterone, abnormal uterine bleeding or significant diabetes/metabolic disease.

sourceReview: Endocrine Society/International PCOS Network 2026: PMOS name change
Monash Centre for Health Research and Implementation: PMOS guideline resources

conditions.name: Severe androgen excess / postmenopausal hyperandrogenism

fields.investigations: Measure testosterone, SHBG with a free-testosterone index, androstenedione, DHEAS, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, oestradiol, LH and FSH; ask specifically about exogenous testosterone exposure and screen for Cushing syndrome only when clinically indicated. Prefer/confirm significant testosterone elevation with LC-MS/MS. Testosterone >5 nmol/L warrants urgent ovarian/adrenal imaging. Predominant testosterone excess suggests an ovarian source; marked DHEAS/androstenedione elevation raises adrenal suspicion. Small ovarian androgen-secreting tumours can be occult on imaging.
fields.treatment: Treat the cause. Androgen-secreting ovarian/adrenal tumours usually require surgical assessment; postmenopausal ovarian hyperthecosis is commonly treated with bilateral oophorectomy. If ovarian surgery is declined or contraindicated, specialist GnRH suppression may reduce ovarian androgen production; spironolactone/finasteride can improve symptoms but do not remove an underlying tumour.
fields.escalation: Urgent endocrine/gynaecology assessment for rapid onset/progression, overt virilisation, testosterone >5 nmol/L or suspected neoplastic androgen excess; arrange ovarian and/or adrenal imaging according to the biochemical pattern.
fields.mimics: PMOS, ovarian hyperthecosis, androgen-secreting ovarian tumour, adrenal tumour, non-classic CAH, Cushing syndrome, severe insulin-resistance syndromes and prescribed/inadvertently transferred exogenous androgens.
fields.redFlags: New or rapidly progressive postmenopausal hirsutism, deepening voice, clitoromegaly, rapidly progressive androgenic alopecia, increased muscle mass, erythrocytosis, pelvic/adrenal mass or severe biochemical androgen excess.

sourceReview: Society for Endocrinology Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation of Androgen Excess in Women, 2025
Endocrine Society/International PCOS Network PMOS resources

conditions.name: Coxsackie / enterovirus infection

fields.investigations: Typical hand-foot-and-mouth disease/herpangina is clinical: fever/sore throat, painful oral ulcers and vesicles on hands/feet; no routine tests. If severe/atypical, neonatal, CNS or cardiac features, discuss targeted enterovirus PCR.
fields.treatment: Supportive: fluids, soft/cool foods, paracetamol or ibuprofen if suitable; no antibiotics for uncomplicated viral disease and no routine antiviral treatment.
fields.escalation: Same-day/ED if dehydration, sepsis, meningism/encephalopathy, neonatal illness, immunocompromise, or suspected myocarditis/pericarditis (chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations/syncope).
fields.mimics: HSV gingivostomatitis, aphthous ulcers, chickenpox, scarlet fever, mpox, meningococcal disease; pleurodynia can mimic ACS, PE or pneumonia.
fields.redFlags: Unable to maintain fluids/low urine, altered consciousness or meningism, rapidly worsening systemic illness, chest pain with dyspnoea/palpitations/syncope, or a febrile/unwell neonate.

sourceReview: NHS: Hand, foot and mouth disease
Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust: Enterovirus PCR clinical indications

conditions.name: Costochondritis

fields.investigations: Clinical after excluding serious chest-pain causes: localised parasternal pain is reproducible by palpation and worse with movement/deep inspiration. Reproducibility supports the diagnosis but does not itself exclude ACS; investigate cardiac/pulmonary causes according to risk and presentation.
fields.treatment: Reassure, modify provoking activity and consider local heat; paracetamol. If an NSAID is suitable, Tayside first-choice ibuprofen at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time (e.g. 200–400 mg up to TDS; max 1.2 g/day OTC), assessing GI/renal/CV risk and gastroprotection need.
fields.escalation: Urgent/ED assessment if ACS, PE, aortic dissection, pneumothorax or sepsis is possible; review persistent/recurrent pain, focal swelling (Tietze syndrome), fever/systemic illness or diagnostic uncertainty.
fields.mimics: ACS, pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pneumonia/pleurisy, GORD, intercostal muscle strain, Tietze syndrome, herpes zoster.
fields.redFlags: Pressure/heaviness or exertional pain, radiation to arm/jaw/back, dyspnoea, syncope, haemoptysis, hypoxia, shock, fever/rigors, unequal pulses or rapidly worsening severe pain.

sourceReview: NHS Tayside Area Formulary: NSAIDs — ibuprofen first choice, lowest dose/shortest duration
UK ibuprofen product information / NHS adult dosing

conditions.name: Labyrinthitis / vestibular neuritis

fields.investigations: Acute continuous vertigo lasting days with nausea/gait unsteadiness; labyrinthitis has hearing loss/tinnitus, vestibular neuritis does not. HINTS is for acute vestibular syndrome only and should be performed by a trained clinician; include otoscopy and bedside hearing assessment.
fields.treatment: For severe symptoms, use a vestibular suppressant/antiemetic only briefly (usually no more than 3 days), e.g. prochlorperazine 5 mg TDS if suitable; encourage early mobilisation and vestibular rehabilitation once tolerated.
fields.escalation: Immediate stroke pathway for central signs or unexplained acute vestibular syndrome when trained HINTS is unavailable. Sudden unexplained hearing loss developing over 3 days or less and within the past 30 days requires immediate ENT/ED assessment (within 24 h).
fields.mimics: Posterior circulation stroke, BPPV, Ménière disease, vestibular migraine, acoustic neuroma, otitis media, drug toxicity.
fields.redFlags: New focal neurology, inability to walk unaided/severe truncal ataxia, direction-changing or vertical nystagmus/skew, severe new headache, or sudden unilateral hearing loss.

sourceReview: NICE NG127: Suspected neurological conditions — acute vestibular syndrome/HINTS
NICE NG98: Hearing loss in adults — sudden hearing loss referral
NHS Tayside Area Formulary: vestibular disorders/vertigo

conditions.name: Diabetic foot ulcer / infection

fields.investigations: In any unwell or septic person with diabetes, remove shoes and socks and inspect both feet as a possible infection source. Assess ulcer depth/extent, erythema, discharge, pulses/perfusion and neuropathy; check observations, glucose/ketones, FBC/CRP and U&E. Take appropriate cultures if infected and blood cultures if septic; foot X-ray if deep infection/osteomyelitis is suspected, with MRI if uncertainty remains.
fields.treatment: For limb- or life-threatening diabetic foot disease, give acute sepsis care and antibiotics according to local diabetic-foot guidance; off-load, debride when appropriate, treat ischaemia and optimise glycaemia. Do not give antibiotics for an uninfected diabetic foot ulcer.
fields.escalation: Immediate acute-services assessment and inform the multidisciplinary foot care team for ulceration with fever/sepsis, limb ischaemia, gangrene or suspected deep soft-tissue/bone infection. Other active diabetic foot problems should be referred within 1 working day for specialist triage within a further working day; involve vascular surgery, orthopaedics and microbiology/ID as indicated.
fields.mimics: Acute Charcot arthropathy, cellulitis without ulceration, pressure injury, arterial or venous ulcer, gout, fracture/trauma and vasculitis.
fields.redFlags: Sepsis or systemic deterioration, rapidly spreading infection, critical limb ischaemia/rest pain, gangrene or necrosis, deep infection/abscess, exposed bone or rapidly progressive tissue loss.

sourceReview: NICE NG19: Diabetic foot problems — active problems, urgent referral and infection management
NICE NG19: Diabetic foot infection antimicrobial principles
NHS Tayside diabetic foot pathway teaching, 25 Sep 2026

conditions.name: Acute Charcot arthropathy

fields.investigations: Suspect acute Charcot in diabetes with a unilateral red, hot, swollen foot with or without deformity, especially with peripheral neuropathy or renal failure; pain may be absent. Arrange a weight-bearing X-ray of the affected foot and ankle; consider MRI if the X-ray is normal but suspicion remains.
fields.treatment: Keep the affected foot non-weight-bearing/off-loaded until definitive specialist treatment. The multidisciplinary foot care service usually uses a non-removable off-loading device when suitable; optimise diabetes and ongoing foot protection.
fields.escalation: Refer within 1 working day to the multidisciplinary foot care service for triage within 1 further working day. Use immediate acute pathways instead if there is sepsis, ulceration with limb ischaemia, gangrene or another limb- or life-threatening diabetic foot problem.
fields.mimics: Cellulitis, osteomyelitis, gout, DVT, septic arthritis, fracture/trauma and other causes of a hot swollen foot.
fields.redFlags: A hot swollen neuropathic foot is concerning even without pain or obvious deformity. Ulceration/infection, fever or sepsis, ischaemia/gangrene, fracture or rapidly developing deformity require urgent escalation.

sourceReview: NICE NG19: Charcot arthropathy — recognition, imaging, referral and off-loading
NHS Tayside diabetic foot pathway teaching, 25 Sep 2026

conditions.name: Infant supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)

fields.investigations: ABCDE, assess perfusion and obtain 12-lead ECG/rhythm strip. SVT is typically abrupt, fixed-rate, regular narrow-complex tachycardia, often >220/min in infants, with absent or retrograde P waves; monitor BP and SpO2.
fields.treatment: Haemodynamically stable regular narrow-complex SVT: under clinical monitoring, briefly apply an ice/cold pack to the infant's upper face to trigger the vagal diving reflex. Keep nose and mouth unobstructed; do not submerge the infant or press the eyes. Vagal stimulation temporarily slows AV-nodal conduction and may terminate AV-node-dependent re-entry. Older cooperative children: modified Valsalva.
fields.escalation: If vagal manoeuvres fail, give rapid IV adenosine with ECG monitoring, appropriate access and paediatric support. Decompensated circulatory failure: immediate synchronised cardioversion, starting at 1 J/kg and doubling up to 4 J/kg; do not delay for vagal manoeuvres. Seek paediatric cardiology advice.
fields.mimics: Sinus tachycardia due to fever, pain, dehydration or sepsis (variable rate, usually discernible sinus P waves); atrial flutter, focal atrial tachycardia and ventricular tachycardia.
fields.redFlags: Poor feeding, pallor, lethargy, irritability, diaphoresis, prolonged persistent tachycardia, hypotension, reduced consciousness, hepatomegaly/heart failure or shock.

sourceReview: Resuscitation Council UK 2025 Paediatric Life Support (basic and advanced), tachyarrhythmia section: https://www.resus.org.uk/professional-library/2025-resuscitation-guidelines/paediatric-basic-life-support-guidelines

conditions.name: Perioperative interruption and restart of antiplatelet therapy

fields.investigations: Identify indication (primary vs secondary prevention, ACS, PCI/stent date and complexity), aspirin alone vs DAPT, planned procedure and neuraxial anaesthesia; assess surgical bleeding against stent-thrombosis risk. Discuss recent PCI/ACS or DAPT with cardiology, surgery and anaesthesia.
fields.treatment: Low-bleeding-risk procedures may allow continuation; usually continue aspirin after PCI. If interruption is agreed: clopidogrel at least 5 days (UKCPA generally 7 days for elective clopidogrel monotherapy or neuraxial block); ticagrelor at least 3 days (5 before neuraxial block); prasugrel 7 days. Extremely high bleeding-risk procedures may also require stopping aspirin.
fields.escalation: Defer elective non-cardiac surgery until the recommended DAPT course is complete where feasible. Restart interrupted P2Y12 therapy as soon as haemostasis permits, preferably within 48 hours, following the agreed MDT plan. Do not routinely use heparin/LMWH to bridge antiplatelet interruption; exceptional IV bridging is cardiologist-led.
fields.mimics: Do not confuse antiplatelet interruption with DOAC/warfarin perioperative anticoagulation protocols. Aspirin primary prevention, established vascular disease, and recent coronary stents carry different thrombotic risks; minor procedures may not require treatment interruption.
fields.redFlags: Recent ACS or PCI/stent (especially within 1 month), complex PCI or previous stent thrombosis, stopping both agents in DAPT, neuraxial block before adequate P2Y12 washout, high-risk intracranial surgery, serious postoperative bleeding or new ischaemic chest pain.

sourceReview: UKCPA Handbook of Perioperative Medicines — Dual Antiplatelet Therapy: https://periop-handbook.ukclinicalpharmacy.org/drug/aspirin-as-dual-antiplatelet-therapy/
UKCPA Handbook of Perioperative Medicines — Clopidogrel: https://periop-handbook.ukclinicalpharmacy.org/drug/clopidogrel/

ESC 2022 Guidelines on cardiovascular assessment and management of patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery: https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/non-cardiac-surgery/

conditions.name: Metformin: mechanism of glucose lowering

fields.investigations: For use in type 2 diabetes, monitor HbA1c/glucose, eGFR before initiation and periodically, and vitamin B12 when symptoms or risk factors suggest deficiency. It is a biguanide, not an insulin secretagogue.
fields.treatment: Principal glucose-lowering action: suppress hepatic gluconeogenesis (and glycogenolysis), reducing endogenous glucose output. It also improves peripheral insulin sensitivity/glucose uptake and alters intestinal glucose handling. AMPK and other cellular pathways contribute; no single pathway fully explains all effects. It does not directly stimulate pancreatic insulin release.
fields.escalation: Use renal-adjusted dosing; contraindicated if eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m². Temporarily withhold during significant dehydration, AKI, sepsis or hypoxic illness; suspected metformin-associated lactic acidosis requires emergency assessment and cessation.
fields.mimics: Contrast mechanisms: sulfonylureas stimulate beta-cell insulin secretion (hypoglycaemia risk); SGLT2 inhibitors increase urinary glucose excretion; GLP-1 receptor agonists enhance glucose-dependent insulin release and suppress glucagon. Metformin monotherapy rarely causes hypoglycaemia.
fields.redFlags: Persistent gastrointestinal intolerance, symptomatic B12 deficiency (neuropathy or macrocytic anaemia), severe renal impairment, vomiting/dehydration, or acidotic breathing with abdominal pain and lethargy suggesting lactic acidosis.

sourceReview: UK electronic medicines compendium (eMC), Metformin Hydrochloride 500 mg SmPC, sections 4.2-4.4 and 5.1 (updated July 2025): https://www.medicines.org.uk/emc/product/13959/smpc
Rena G et al., The mechanisms of action of metformin (Diabetologia 2017): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28776086/

conditions.name: Zika virus: travel prevention and absence of a vaccine

fields.investigations: Travel and mosquito/sexual exposure history; often asymptomatic. Symptomatic Zika may cause mild fever, rash, arthralgia and conjunctivitis. Assess pregnancy status; discuss appropriate Zika testing with infection specialists/UKHSA if indicated. Urgently exclude malaria in a febrile traveller returning from a malaria-risk area.
fields.treatment: No licensed Zika vaccine, preventive drug or specific antiviral treatment. Prevention is daytime Aedes bite avoidance: 50% DEET repellent if suitable (including pregnancy; age over 2 months), covering clothing and insecticide-treated nets/screens. Symptomatic care: fluids and paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs until dengue is excluded.
fields.escalation: Pregnant travellers or those planning pregnancy need pre-travel risk discussion; during major outbreaks consider deferring non-essential travel. After possible exposure in pregnancy, seek midwife/GP assessment even if asymptomatic. For pregnancy planning, UKHSA advises protection against conception/sexual transmission for 2 months after a female traveller's last possible exposure and 3 months after male or both partners' exposure; use barriers throughout pregnancy if a partner has been exposed.
fields.mimics: Dengue, chikungunya, malaria, rubella, measles and other viral exanthems; distinguish Zika (no vaccine) from vaccine-preventable yellow fever or Japanese encephalitis.
fields.redFlags: Pregnancy with possible Zika exposure (congenital Zika syndrome/microcephaly risk), severe neurological symptoms such as ascending weakness (Guillain-Barré), dehydration or haemodynamic instability, or fever after travel to a malaria-endemic area.

sourceReview: UKHSA — Zika virus: preventing infection by sexual transmission: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/zika-virus-preventing-infection-by-sexual-transmission
NaTHNaC — Insect and tick bite avoidance: https://travelhealthpro.org.uk/factsheet/38/insect-and-tick-bite-avoidance

conditions.name: Travel vaccinations: indications by destination and traveller risk

fields.investigations: Pre-travel assessment: destination/region, route, season, duration, activities, accommodation, prior vaccines, age, pregnancy, immunosuppression, medication and allergies. Check NaTHNaC TravelHealthPro country recommendations and UK routine immunisation status; book ideally 4–6 weeks before departure.
fields.treatment: Update routine vaccines (e.g. MMR and tetanus/diphtheria/polio) as indicated. Offer destination/exposure-specific vaccines after risk assessment: hepatitis A, typhoid, cholera, hepatitis B, rabies, Japanese encephalitis, tick-borne encephalitis and yellow fever where appropriate. Certain vaccines/proof of vaccination may be entry requirements; confirm with destination guidance.
fields.escalation: Seek travel clinic/specialist advice for pregnancy, immunosuppression, complex medical conditions, young infants, vaccine allergies, live-vaccine precautions or yellow fever certification. Last-minute travellers still benefit from assessment; plan multi-dose schedules and advise if immunity will be incomplete.
fields.mimics: Vaccination is distinct from malaria chemoprophylaxis and mosquito-bite precautions. No vaccine is available against Zika, and many travel infections require food/water or insect-bite prevention even when other vaccines have been administered.
fields.redFlags: Live vaccines may be contraindicated in severe immunosuppression and generally avoided in pregnancy; unavoidable exposure to yellow fever requires specialist risk assessment. Unvaccinated measles exposure, travel to high-risk outbreak regions, or post-travel fever (especially malaria risk) requires prompt clinical action.

sourceReview: UKHSA — Malaria prevention guidelines for travellers from the UK 2026: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/malaria-prevention-guidelines-for-travellers-from-the-uk-2026/general-issues

conditions.name: Atrial fibrillation stroke prevention: CHA2DS2-VASc and anticoagulation threshold

fields.investigations: For confirmed AF (paroxysmal, persistent or permanent) or atrial flutter, calculate CHA2DS2-VASc: C heart failure (1); H hypertension (1); A2 age ≥75 (2); D diabetes (1); S2 prior stroke/TIA/systemic embolus (2); V vascular disease (1); A age 65–74 (1); Sc female sex (1). Also assess ORBIT bleeding risk, FBC, U&E/renal function, LFTs and interactions.
fields.treatment: NICE NG196: offer a DOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban or rivaroxaban) when CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2, taking bleeding risk into account; consider a DOAC in men scoring 1. Do not anticoagulate people <65 with no risk factors other than sex (0 men, 1 women). If a DOAC is unsuitable, consider a vitamin K antagonist. Aspirin monotherapy is NOT AF stroke prophylaxis.
fields.escalation: Make a shared decision using stroke risk, ORBIT bleeding risk, comorbidities and contraindications; calculate Cockcroft–Gault creatinine clearance for DOAC dosing. Review risks and anticoagulant treatment at least annually, and sooner if risk changes. After cardioversion or successful ablation, do not stop anticoagulation solely because AF is no longer detectable.
fields.mimics: CHA2DS2-VASc predicts ischaemic stroke/systemic embolism, not bleeding (ORBIT). AF symptoms or ventricular rate do not determine thromboembolic risk. Mechanical prosthetic valves or moderate/severe mitral stenosis need specific anticoagulant guidance rather than routine DOAC selection.
fields.redFlags: Previous stroke/TIA, age ≥75, very recent embolic event, possible contraindication such as active major bleeding, and renal impairment affecting DOAC selection/dose. Age or falls risk alone is not a reason to withhold anticoagulation.

sourceReview: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, sections 1.2, 1.6 and 1.11: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196/chapter/recommendations

conditions.name: CHA2DS2-VASc versus ORBIT: stroke and bleeding risk assessment

fields.investigations: Calculate both scores when considering/continuing AF anticoagulation. CHA2DS2-VASc = stroke risk; ORBIT = major bleeding risk. ORBIT: age ≥75 (1); reduced Hb/anaemia or low haematocrit (2); prior bleeding (2); eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m² (1); concomitant antiplatelet therapy (1). ORBIT 0–2 low, 3 medium, ≥4 high bleeding risk.
fields.treatment: Use CHA2DS2-VASc to guide anticoagulation decisions (NICE: offer DOAC if ≥2; consider in men if 1). Use ORBIT to communicate bleeding risk, correct modifiable risks (uncontrolled BP, antiplatelets/NSAIDs, harmful alcohol use; poor INR control on warfarin), and plan monitoring. An elevated ORBIT score is not in itself a contraindication to anticoagulation.
fields.escalation: Review anticoagulant treatment and stroke/bleeding risks at least annually or after a clinical change, bleeding event or deterioration in renal function. Severe unexplained anaemia, recurrent major bleeding or difficult combinations of antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy merit specialist review; urgent assessment for active major bleeding.
fields.mimics: Do not swap the two scores: HAS-BLED is another bleeding score, but NICE favours ORBIT for prediction of absolute major bleeding risk. Anticoagulation selection is not driven by AF rate/rhythm symptoms or a successful return to sinus rhythm alone.
fields.redFlags: Active major bleeding, intracranial haemorrhage symptoms, unexplained marked anaemia, uncontrolled severe hypertension, renal deterioration or dual antithrombotic therapy increasing bleeding risk. Do not deny anticoagulation solely for age, falls or a high ORBIT score.

sourceReview: NICE NG196, section 1.2 Assessment of stroke and bleeding risks: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196/chapter/recommendations

NICE NG196 evidence review E and F: risk tools for predicting bleeding: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196/evidence/e-and-f-risk-stratification-tools-for-predicting-bleeding-in-people-with-atrial-fibrillation-pdf-9081923441
O'Brien et al. ORBIT bleeding score, European Heart Journal 2015: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4670965/

conditions.name: DVLA: notification duties and Group 1 versus Group 2

fields.investigations: Establish exact licence categories, professional driving, diagnosis, symptoms, treatment and functional impairment; consult DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (DVA for Northern Ireland).
fields.treatment: Group 1 covers cars/motorcycles. A medical driving restriction does not always require DVLA notification: document both decisions separately.
fields.escalation: Group 2 covers lorries/buses and has stricter thresholds and relicensing tests; some Group 1 permissions do not apply to Group 2.
fields.mimics: Driver normally has the legal duty to notify DVLA; the clinician must advise and document. If a patient continues to drive despite serious risk, follow GMC disclosure guidance.
fields.redFlags: Stop driving when a condition or medication impairs safe control even before DVLA responds. Do not assume 'not notifiable' means 'safe to drive'.

conditions.name: DVLA: aortic aneurysm size and driving

fields.investigations: Identify aneurysm diameter, aortic segment, syndromic aortopathy, symptoms, repair status and interval imaging; ensure regular clinical review.
fields.treatment: Group 1: <6.0 cm may drive without notification; 6.0–6.4 cm may drive but notify and undergo annual licensing review; ≥6.5 cm stop and notify.
fields.escalation: Group 2: ≤5.5 cm may drive but must notify; >5.5 cm stop and notify. Descending thoracic/abdominal aneurysm also needs appropriate cardiac functional testing.
fields.mimics: Do not substitute the usual 5.5 cm elective AAA-repair threshold for DVLA Group 1 cut-offs; Marfan and bicuspid aortopathy follow separate rules.
fields.redFlags: Symptomatic aneurysm, suspected dissection/rupture, rapidly enlarging aneurysm or threshold breach: stop driving and urgent assessment as clinically indicated.

conditions.name: DVLA: severe hypertension thresholds

fields.investigations: Repeat resting BP and check symptoms/end-organ damage; distinguish sustained hypertension from malignant hypertension.
fields.treatment: Group 1: ordinary hypertension need not be notified. Malignant hypertension (≥180 systolic or ≥110 diastolic WITH progressive organ damage) requires stopping until controlled; no DVLA notification ordinarily.
fields.escalation: Group 2: sustained resting BP ≥180 systolic OR ≥100 diastolic means stop and notify; malignant hypertension also means stop and notify. Resume only after control and absence of impairing treatment effects.
fields.mimics: Group 1 does not have an automatic ban at an isolated 180/100 reading; malignant hypertension requires organ damage.
fields.redFlags: Headache plus neurological deficit, chest pain, acute pulmonary oedema or renal injury merits urgent assessment for hypertensive emergency.

conditions.name: DVLA: acute coronary syndrome / myocardial infarction

fields.investigations: Confirm PCI success, urgent further revascularisation plan, LVEF before discharge and other disqualifying symptoms.
fields.treatment: Group 1: after ACS successful PCI, may resume after 1 week only if no urgent revascularisation planned within 4 weeks, LVEF ≥40% and no other disqualification; otherwise after 4 weeks. Need not notify DVLA.
fields.escalation: Group 2: stop and notify for all ACS; potential relicensing after ≥6 weeks if LVEF ≥40%, required functional cardiac testing passed and no other disqualification.
fields.mimics: Uncomplicated ACS with successful PCI differs from ACS managed medically; successful PCI is not itself sufficient without the LVEF and planned-treatment criteria.
fields.redFlags: Recurrent chest pain, syncope, arrhythmia or heart failure may independently prevent safe driving.

conditions.name: DVLA: elective PCI and coronary bypass

fields.investigations: Clarify elective PCI versus ACS-related PCI versus CABG; assess complications, angina, LVEF and revascularisation status.
fields.treatment: Group 1: elective PCI requires ≥1 week off; CABG ≥4 weeks off. Usually no notification if uncomplicated and no other disqualification.
fields.escalation: Group 2: elective PCI ≥6 weeks off; CABG ≥3 months off. Must notify and meet LVEF ≥40%, functional cardiac test and other licensing criteria.
fields.mimics: Never use the elective PCI interval to clear someone after a myocardial infarction; apply the ACS rules when intervention treats ACS.
fields.redFlags: Residual angina, arrhythmia, poor ventricular function or incomplete recovery may require longer restriction.

conditions.name: DVLA: incapacitating arrhythmia and pacemaker

fields.investigations: Establish syncope/presyncope or inability to control a vehicle, arrhythmia treatment and device type; distinguish pacemaker from ICD.
fields.treatment: Group 1: incapacitating/likely incapacitating arrhythmia: stop and notify; resume ≥4 weeks after last event only if cause treated and no likely recurrence. Pacemaker insertion/box change: ≥1 week off; notify insertion, not routine box change.
fields.escalation: Group 2: incapacitating arrhythmia: stop and notify; consider licence only after ≥3 months without likely incapacity, cause treated and LVEF ≥40%. Pacemaker insertion/box change: ≥6 weeks off; notify insertion, not box change.
fields.mimics: Stable asymptomatic AF is not automatically subject to the 4-week incapacitating-arrhythmia restriction; correlate rhythm with symptoms.
fields.redFlags: Syncope from arrhythmia, recurrent VT, symptomatic bradycardia or new ICD indication merits immediate driving review.

conditions.name: DVLA: implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD)

fields.investigations: Check primary versus secondary prevention implant, ventricular arrhythmia, appropriate shocks and device interrogation history.
fields.treatment: Group 1: secondary-prevention ICD generally ≥6 months off and notify. Prophylactic ICD in asymptomatic patient: ≥1 month off and notify. Appropriate ICD shock for VT/VF generally restarts a 6-month restriction.
fields.escalation: Group 2: ICD implanted OR clinically indicated/recommended is a permanent bar to licensing; stop and notify, even if implantation is declined.
fields.mimics: Do not confuse ICD rules with pacemaker rules or assume prophylactic devices have the same Group 1 restriction as secondary prevention.
fields.redFlags: Appropriate ICD therapy, sustained VT/VF, loss of consciousness or new device malfunction requires specialist assessment.

conditions.name: DVLA: first seizure and established epilepsy

fields.investigations: Clarify provoked/unprovoked event, previous seizures, awake/asleep pattern, EEG/MRI, neurologist opinion and antiseizure medication.
fields.treatment: Group 1: first unprovoked seizure: stop and notify; usually 6 months off, 12 if increased recurrence risk. Established epilepsy: usually 12 months seizure-free before driving; permitted-seizure exceptions exist.
fields.escalation: Group 2: first unprovoked seizure: ≥5 years off and no antiseizure drugs in preceding 5 years, with favourable neurologist risk assessment. Established epilepsy: generally 10 years seizure-free without antiseizure drugs.
fields.mimics: Do not apply a universal 6-month rule to recurrent epilepsy, provoked seizures or solely nocturnal seizure concessions.
fields.redFlags: Any new seizure while licensed ordinarily requires immediate cessation and notification unless a DVLA-recognised permitted-seizure rule applies.

conditions.name: DVLA: stroke and TIA

fields.investigations: Determine TIA versus stroke, date of last event, recurrence, residual motor/visual/cognitive deficits and seizure history.
fields.treatment: Group 1: TIA stop for 1 month, normally no DVLA notification. Stroke stop for ≥1 month; notify if a relevant deficit persists at 1 month. Resume only after satisfactory clinical recovery.
fields.escalation: Group 2: stroke or TIA: stop and notify; licence refused/revoked for 1 year, then specialist/DVLA assessment of residual impairment and risk factors.
fields.mimics: Amaurosis fugax/retinal artery occlusion may follow cerebrovascular guidance; recurrent episodes and associated seizures may trigger additional rules.
fields.redFlags: Visual field loss, cognitive impairment, recurrent TIA or post-stroke seizure may independently disqualify driving.

conditions.name: DVLA: reflex vasovagal syncope and warning symptoms

fields.investigations: Make a positive diagnosis of reflex syncope; assess reliable prodrome long enough to stop safely, avoidable provocation, recurrence within 24 months and occurrence at wheel.
fields.treatment: Group 1: single reflex syncope with reliable prodrome NOT at wheel can continue driving without notifying. If at wheel: 1 month off, ordinarily no notification. Without reliable prodrome, stop and notify; often 3 months if not avoidably provoked.
fields.escalation: Group 2: must notify even for a single episode with reliable warning; if no avoidable trigger or event at wheel, typically 3 months off with reliable warning, 12 months without warning, plus specialist report.
fields.mimics: Brief light-headedness is not necessarily syncope; if cause cannot be confidently attributed, apply unexplained loss-of-consciousness rules instead.
fields.redFlags: Sudden syncope without warning, syncope while driving, recurrent episodes, exertional syncope or abnormal ECG requires careful exclusion of cardiac causes.

conditions.name: DVLA: unexplained blackout versus cough syncope

fields.investigations: Document witnesses, prodrome, triggers, seizure markers, ECG, orthostatic findings and number/timing of episodes.
fields.treatment: Group 1: single unexplained loss of consciousness without seizure markers: stop and notify, 6 months off; recurrent episodes: generally 12 months. Cough syncope: stop and notify; 6 months after one event, 12 months after multiple events.
fields.escalation: Group 2: one unexplained blackout requires 12 months off and notification; multiple unexplained episodes may require 5 years. Cough syncope: 12 months off after one episode, 5 years after multiple episodes over 5 years; notify in all cases.
fields.mimics: Do not diagnose vasovagal syncope without convincing evidence merely to shorten restrictions; cough syncope remains relevant even after cough resolves.
fields.redFlags: Tongue biting, post-ictal confusion, exertional collapse, cardiac symptoms or blackouts at wheel warrant specialist investigation.

conditions.name: DVLA: insulin-treated diabetes and glucose monitoring

fields.investigations: Assess insulin use, hypoglycaemia awareness, severe events, visual/neurological complications and documented glucose self-monitoring.
fields.treatment: Group 1: must notify; licence may be granted if adequate awareness, no disqualifying severe hypoglycaemia pattern and appropriate monitoring. Check glucose before first journey and at least every 2 hours driving.
fields.escalation: Group 2: notify and stop Group 2 driving on starting insulin until DVLA licensing decision; annual specialist assessment, full hypo awareness, no severe hypo in past 12 months and at least 4 weeks stored readings. Check at least twice daily, plus before driving and every 2 hours.
fields.mimics: CGM can be used if approved for non-adjunctive monitoring, but carry a finger-prick meter as backup; alarms do not replace symptom awareness.
fields.redFlags: Severe hypoglycaemia, hypoglycaemia unawareness or inability to monitor safely requires prompt driving cessation/advice.

conditions.name: DVLA: severe hypoglycaemia and impaired awareness

fields.investigations: Severe hypoglycaemia means needing another person's assistance; record daytime versus sleep episodes and whether it occurred while driving.
fields.treatment: Group 1: ≥2 episodes while awake within 12 months: stop and notify; any severe event at wheel: stop and notify. Nocturnal episodes in established sleep generally do not count unless awareness is concerning.
fields.escalation: Group 2: any severe episode, including during sleep, means stop and notify. No severe hypoglycaemia in past 12 months is a licensing requirement.
fields.mimics: Impaired hypo awareness: stop and notify for both groups; Group 1 may resume after clinical confirmation awareness restored; Group 2 requires full awareness.
fields.redFlags: Do not equate one self-treated low glucose reading with severe hypoglycaemia; recurrent episodes or inability to detect lows threaten driving safety.

conditions.name: DVLA: non-insulin diabetes treatment

fields.investigations: Identify diet alone, sulfonylurea/glinide versus non-hypoglycaemia-inducing agents, hypoglycaemia and diabetic complications.
fields.treatment: Group 1: diet alone, metformin, SGLT2, GLP-1, DPP-4 drugs and generally sulfonylureas may drive without DVLA notification if standards met.
fields.escalation: Group 2: diet alone no notification. Drug-treated diabetes (including metformin or SGLT2/GLP-1 therapy) requires notification; sulfonylurea/glinide users must meet extra glucose-monitoring and hypo-awareness criteria.
fields.mimics: Do not assume insulin is the only diabetes treatment relevant to Group 2 notification.
fields.redFlags: Any severe hypo, impaired awareness, disabling neuropathy or visual complication triggers separate DVLA review.

conditions.name: DVLA: minimum visual acuity and visual field

fields.investigations: Test binocular Snellen acuity with correction, number-plate reading and binocular field; use formal Esterman field testing when required.
fields.treatment: Group 1: read modern number plate at 20 m, binocular (or only eye) acuity at least 6/12 and horizontal visual field at least 120°, extending ≥50° each side, without significant central defect.
fields.escalation: Group 2: acuity ≥6/7.5 better eye and ≥6/60 worse eye; continuous field ≥160° with ≥70° each side, 30° up/down and no central 30° defect; other optical criteria also apply.
fields.mimics: Meeting Snellen acuity does not compensate for hemianopia or central field loss; historical Group 2 grandfather-rights exceptions are limited.
fields.redFlags: Failure to meet statutory eyesight standards means stop driving and notify DVLA.

conditions.name: DVLA: diplopia and monocular vision

fields.investigations: Differentiate new diplopia from adapted monocular vision; assess cause, visual acuity, field and impact on navigation.
fields.treatment: Group 1: diplopia requires stop and notify; may drive only after DVLA accepts satisfactory control (e.g. prism or patch with monocular standard met). Monocular vision may be licensed after successful adaptation if standards met.
fields.escalation: Group 2: insuperable diplopia cannot be licensed; patching is not accepted. Monocular vision usually excludes Group 2 except narrowly defined historic entitlements.
fields.mimics: Driving with a patch is not universally valid; Group 2 vision standards remain stricter even if diplopia seems controlled.
fields.redFlags: New-onset double vision can signal acute neurological disease and should be clinically assessed urgently as appropriate.

conditions.name: DVLA: obstructive sleep apnoea and excessive sleepiness

fields.investigations: Assess driving-relevant sleepiness, sleep attacks, near misses, AHI severity, CPAP adherence and other sedating causes.
fields.treatment: Group 1: mild OSA (AHI <15) or suspected OSA with excessive sleepiness: stop until controlled; notify if not controlled within 3 months. Moderate/severe OSA (AHI ≥15) WITH excessive sleepiness: stop and notify; resume only after effective control and DVLA criteria.
fields.escalation: Group 2: same notification trigger but stricter follow-up: moderate/severe OSA with excessive sleepiness needs documented control, adherence and at least annual review; Group 1 review at least every 3 years.
fields.mimics: OSA diagnosis/AHI alone does not establish the sleepiness restriction: assess excessive sleepiness likely to impair driving.
fields.redFlags: Microsleeps, sleepiness at wheel, untreated sleepy OSA or sedative co-prescribing make driving unsafe.

conditions.name: DVLA: dementia, Parkinson disease and cognitive impairment

fields.investigations: Assess insight, memory, executive function, attention, navigation, motor control, fluctuation and potential formal driving assessment.
fields.treatment: Group 1: dementia must be notified; early slowly progressive dementia may be licensed after DVLA assessment, often annual review. Parkinson disease and MS must be notified but driving can continue if control is safe and DVLA permits.
fields.escalation: Group 2: dementia: stop and notify, licence refused/revoked. Other neurological disorders need DVLA notification and specialist assessment; severe motor variability or disability may prevent licensing.
fields.mimics: Diagnosis of dementia is not automatically an immediate Group 1 driving ban, but absence of insight or disorientation strongly argues against fitness.
fields.redFlags: Getting lost, significant inattention, poor judgement, falls from uncontrolled movement or inability to use controls needs safety action.

conditions.name: DVLA: severe depression, psychosis and mania

fields.investigations: Assess cognitive impairment, suicidal thoughts, agitation, insight, treatment stability and medication-related sedation.
fields.treatment: Group 1: mild/moderate depression without driving impairment need not be notified. Severe depression/anxiety: stop and notify; consider licence after ≥3 months stable. Acute psychosis and stable mania typically need ≥3 months stable plus specialist input.
fields.escalation: Group 2: severe depression/anxiety generally ≥6 months stable; psychosis or mania generally ≥12 months well and stable with specialist support. Stop and notify DVLA while unfit.
fields.mimics: Diagnostic label alone is not decisive for mild depression; acuity, insight, relapse risk and medication effects control the decision.
fields.redFlags: Suicidal intent at wheel, active psychosis/mania or medication impairing alertness means no driving.

conditions.name: DVLA: alcohol misuse and alcohol dependence

fields.investigations: Determine persistent misuse versus dependence with high-risk features: withdrawal seizure or medically assisted alcohol withdrawal; assess sobriety and complications.
fields.treatment: Group 1: persistent misuse/dependence without high-risk features: stop, notify; ≥6 months controlled drinking or abstinence. High-risk-feature dependence: ≥1 year abstinence before relicensing consideration.
fields.escalation: Group 2: persistent misuse/dependence without high-risk features: stop, notify; ≥1 year controlled drinking or abstinence. High-risk dependence: ≥3 years abstinence.
fields.mimics: High-risk physiological dependence has much stricter abstinence standards than persistent misuse; one episode of intoxication is not synonymous with dependence.
fields.redFlags: Alcohol-related seizures, cognitive dysfunction, sedating co-medication, drink-driving or relapses may impose additional restrictions.

conditions.name: DVLA: sedating medicines, anaesthesia and driving

fields.investigations: Review opioids, benzodiazepines, hypnotics, sedating antihistamines, antipsychotics, new doses, anaesthesia and the driver's ability to safely operate controls.
fields.treatment: Group 1: do not drive when impaired by medicine, excessive sleepiness, sedative effects or post-operative limitations; no universal DVLA notification simply because a sedative was prescribed.
fields.escalation: Group 2: same prohibition on impairment, with stricter occupational medical standards; check diagnosis-specific notification and post-procedure rules.
fields.mimics: An allowed prescribed medicine is not permission to drive while impaired; sedative interactions and dose changes can make otherwise stable patients unsafe.
fields.redFlags: Sleepiness, reduced reaction time, confusion, impaired coordination or inability to emergency brake means stop driving and assess.

conditions.name: DVLA: sudden disabling vertigo

fields.investigations: Assess whether dizziness is sudden, unprovoked, sufficiently severe to prevent safe control, and likely to recur.
fields.treatment: Group 1: sudden unheralded disabling dizziness: stop on presentation and notify DVLA; relicensing may follow satisfactory symptom control.
fields.escalation: Group 2: stop and notify; if underlying diagnosis predicts recurrence, generally requires 1 year asymptomatic and fully controlled before reapplication.
fields.mimics: Brief positional vertigo with sufficient warning is not necessarily the same as sudden, disabling, unprecipitated dizziness; apply the specific clinical criteria.
fields.redFlags: Vertigo with new focal neurology, ataxia, diplopia, severe headache or inability to walk warrants urgent assessment for central pathology.

conditions.name: DVLA: angina at rest, with emotion or driving

fields.investigations: Ask whether angina occurs at rest, with emotion or at the wheel; assess control on treatment, cardiovascular events and Group 2 functional test eligibility.
fields.treatment: Group 1: stop driving if angina occurs at rest, with emotion or while driving; resume when satisfactorily controlled. DVLA notification is not required for uncomplicated angina.
fields.escalation: Group 2: must notify DVLA and stop driving if symptomatic; relicensing may be considered after ≥6 weeks without angina AND meeting exercise or other cardiac functional test criteria.
fields.mimics: Do not automatically impose an ACS 1-week or 4-week restriction on stable angina; follow ACS rules instead if MI/ACS has occurred.
fields.redFlags: New rest chest pain or suspected ACS warrants emergency assessment; uncontrolled angina at the wheel or with minimal exertion is unsafe for driving.

conditions.name: Cerebral palsy: early recognition

fields.investigations: Assess developmental history, asymmetry of spontaneous movements, posture, tone and motor milestones; consider specialist neuroimaging following assessment.
fields.treatment: Early multidisciplinary assessment and intervention (physiotherapy/occupational therapy) should not await a definitive cerebral palsy diagnosis.
fields.escalation: Refer suspected cerebral palsy urgently to a child development service for multidisciplinary assessment (NICE NG62).
fields.mimics: Other causes of unilateral weakness or motor delay, including peripheral nerve injury and progressive neurological disorders.
fields.redFlags: Hand preference before 12 months, asymmetric movements, abnormal tone, delayed head control, not sitting at 8 months (corrected age) or not walking by 18 months.

sourceReview: NICE NG62: Cerebral palsy in under 25s

conditions.name: Developmental regression: recognition and escalation

fields.investigations: Clarify exactly which previously acquired skills were lost and the time course; assess motor, language, social and neurological findings. Consider creatine kinase in boys with motor delay/regression.
fields.treatment: Investigate the underlying cause; provide supportive developmental care while specialist assessment proceeds.
fields.escalation: Refer motor regression to paediatric neurology or neurodevelopmental services; new-onset gait abnormality requires immediate acute paediatric assessment (NICE NG127).
fields.mimics: Hearing impairment may resemble language regression; autism can involve language/social regression; consider neuromuscular, metabolic and neurodegenerative disease.
fields.redFlags: True loss of acquired skills, progressive weakness, new gait abnormality, seizures or other new neurological signs.

sourceReview: NICE CG128: Autism spectrum disorder in under 19s

conditions.name: Delayed motor milestones: NICE referral thresholds

fields.investigations: Assess sitting and independent walking, tone, symmetry and other developmental domains; use corrected age for prematurity. Consider creatine kinase in boys with motor delay.
fields.treatment: Arrange appropriate developmental assessment and early physiotherapy/occupational therapy input according to findings.
fields.escalation: Refer children not sitting unsupported by 8 months (corrected age), not walking independently by 15 months in girls or 18 months in boys, or showing early hand asymmetry (NICE NG127).
fields.mimics: Normal variation, prematurity, orthopaedic disorders, neuromuscular disease and cerebral palsy.
fields.redFlags: Loss of motor skills, progressive weakness, asymmetric movement or new-onset gait abnormality (immediate assessment).

conditions.name: Nocturnal enuresis: assessment and first-line management

fields.investigations: Ask frequency, duration and whether ever dry for ≥6 months (primary versus secondary); assess daytime urgency, frequency, dysuria, constipation, fluid intake, psychosocial factors and snoring. Urinalysis is not routine unless recent onset, daytime symptoms, illness or suspected UTI/diabetes.
fields.treatment: From age 5, reassure and offer practical measures: adequate daytime fluids, regular daytime and bedtime toileting, treat constipation and reward agreed behaviours (not dry nights). If treatment is desired, offer an enuresis alarm when appropriate; desmopressin if rapid/short-term dryness is needed or alarm unsuitable.
fields.escalation: Review alarm response after 4 weeks; continue if early improvement and assess after 3 months. Refer if red flags, significant daytime symptoms, suspected underlying disorder or failure of appropriate treatment.
fields.mimics: Non-monosymptomatic enuresis (daytime lower urinary tract symptoms), UTI, constipation, diabetes mellitus/insipidus, sleep-disordered breathing, and psychosocial stress.
fields.redFlags: New-onset bedwetting after sustained dryness, polyuria/polydipsia or weight loss, recurrent UTI, neurological signs, abnormal urinary stream or significant daytime urinary symptoms. Desmopressin requires fluid restriction from 1 hour before until 8 hours after dosing.

conditions.name: Paediatric asthma: age-specific step-up and MART

fields.investigations: Assess daytime/night-time symptoms, reliever use, activity limitation and exacerbations; review inhaler technique, adherence, triggers and comorbidities before stepping up. In children aged 5–16, use objective tests to support diagnosis where feasible.
fields.treatment: Age 5–11: if uncontrolled on low-dose ICS maintenance plus as-needed SABA, consider low-dose paediatric ICS/formoterol MART if able to manage it and an appropriate licensed device is available; otherwise follow the age-specific conventional add-on pathway. MART uses the same ICS/formoterol inhaler for maintenance and relief; not all ICS/LABA inhalers are suitable.
fields.escalation: If uncontrolled on low-dose MART, consider moderate-dose MART according to NG245 and licensing; refer for specialist assessment if still uncontrolled. Under 5s follow a separate age-specific pathway, not routine MART. Acute severe/life-threatening features require emergency management.
fields.mimics: Poor technique or adherence, viral-induced wheeze, dysfunctional breathing, upper-airway disease, reflux or alternative respiratory diagnosis.
fields.redFlags: Recurrent severe attacks, hospital attendance, frequent reliever use, nocturnal symptoms, hypoxia, exhaustion, silent chest or inability to speak. Check device age licensing and local formulary before prescribing MART.

sourceReview: NICE/BTS/SIGN NG245: Asthma diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management (2024), children aged 5–11

conditions.name: Asthma under 5: ICS trial and step-up

fields.investigations: Diagnosis is clinical; review interval symptoms, severe wheeze episodes, alternative diagnoses, triggers, adherence and inhaler technique. Objective testing is difficult under 5; attempt if symptoms persist at age 5.
fields.treatment: For suspected asthma with interval symptoms or severe episodes, trial twice-daily paediatric low-dose ICS plus as-needed SABA for 8–12 weeks. If resolved, consider stopping and review after 3 months; if recurrent, restart ICS and titrate up to moderate dose as needed.
fields.escalation: If no response to initial trial despite checking technique, adherence, environment and diagnosis, refer. If uncontrolled on moderate-dose ICS, trial LTRA for 8–12 weeks; stop if ineffective and refer. MART is not routine under 5.
fields.mimics: Preschool viral wheeze, foreign body, airway malacia, reflux/aspiration, recurrent infection and other causes of wheeze.
fields.redFlags: Hospital admission or ≥2 ED attendances for wheeze in 12 months warrants respiratory paediatric referral; severe respiratory distress, exhaustion, cyanosis or hypoxia require emergency assessment.

sourceReview: NICE/BTS/SIGN NG245: asthma pharmacological management (2024; updated 2025)

conditions.name: Asthma age 12 and over: AIR to MART

fields.investigations: Assess symptom frequency, nocturnal waking, reliever use, exacerbations, adherence, technique and triggers; check FeNO where possible if uncontrolled.
fields.treatment: Newly diagnosed age ≥12: as-needed low-dose ICS/formoterol AIR. If uncontrolled, offer low-dose MART (same ICS/formoterol inhaler for maintenance and relief); if still uncontrolled, offer moderate-dose MART.
fields.escalation: If uncontrolled despite adherent moderate-dose MART, check FeNO and eosinophils; refer if raised. If neither raised, consider 8–12-week add-on LTRA or LAMA; refer if persistently uncontrolled or high-dose ICS required.
fields.mimics: Poor inhaler technique or adherence, dysfunctional breathing, inducible laryngeal obstruction, rhinitis and alternative diagnoses.
fields.redFlags: Exacerbation requiring oral steroids, frequent reliever use, nocturnal waking or severe attacks. AIR/MART require an appropriate ICS/formoterol device; check licensing and do not use LABA combinations without formoterol as relievers.

sourceReview: NICE/BTS/SIGN NG245: asthma pharmacological management (2024; updated 2025)
